question.knowledge_point: Finding the Range of a Transformed Reciprocal Function
question.worked_solution:
A transformed reciprocal function of the form

$$
f(x)=\frac{a}{bx+c}+d
$$

has the horizontal asymptote $y=d,$ and therefore, its range is

$$
f(x)\in (-\infty ,d)\cup (d,\infty ).
$$

In our case, $d=2.$ Therefore, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2,$ and the range of the function is

$$
f(x)\in (-\infty ,2)\cup (2,\infty ).
$$

The graph $y=f(x)$ is shown below.

question.knowledge_point: Solving for an Unknown Constant in a Transformed Reciprocal Function Given the Domain
question.problem: The domain of the function $f(x)=\frac{4x+3}{5x+2k}$ is $(-\infty ,\frac{2}{5})\cup (\frac{2}{5},\infty ).$ What is the value of $k?$
question.worked_solution:
A reciprocal function is defined for all values of $x$ except for those that make the denominator zero. So, to find the domain, we must exclude all values that make the denominator zero.

Setting the denominator equal to zero and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+2k & =0 \\ 5x & =-2k \\ x & =-\frac{2k}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point that must be excluded from the domain is $x=-\frac{2k}{5}.$ 

On the other hand, we can see that $x=\frac{2}{5}$ is excluded from the domain. Equating this to $-\frac{2k}{5},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2k}{5} & =\frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{k}{5} & =-\frac{1}{5} \\ k & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line When a Component of the Direction Vector is Zero
question.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
question.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-(-1)}{0}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-0}{-1}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+1}{0}=\frac{y-1}{2}=-z,
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{x+1}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $x$ component always maintains the constant value of $x=-1:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1+2t \\ -t\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{x+1}{0}$ part and instead write $x=-1,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{y-1}{2}=-z,\,x=-1
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given Two Points on the Line
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094392/assets/30299b98c822a5b06b332860bafbed4f465a4567a7135dc3257c4c9e40e490fa.png)

Find a Cartesian equation of the line shown in the figure above.
question.worked_solution:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(2,-3,4)$ and $Q(-1,-3,7).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. Let's consider the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ which is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨-1,-3,7⟩-⟨2,-3,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,0,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point $P$ and the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$, we have that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the given line is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{-3}=\frac{y-(-3)}{0}=\frac{z-4}{3}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x-2}{-3}=\frac{y+3}{0}=\frac{z-4}{3}.
$$

But the above equation is problematic because $\frac{y+3}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, in our line, the $y$ component always maintains the constant value of $y=-3.$ For example, our two points $P(2,-3,4)$ and $Q(-1,-3,7)$ both have $y$-coordinates of $y=-3.$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{y+3}{0}$ part and instead write $y=-3,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x-2}{-3}=\frac{z-4}{3},\,y=-3.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of a Nilpotent Matrix
question.worked_solution:
Computing ${K}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{K}^{2} & =K\cdot K \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 16 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 & 16 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, since ${K}^{2}=O,$ the matrix $K$ is a nilpotent matrix of index $2.$ 

We can use this fact to compute ${K}^{6}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{K}^{6} & ={K}^{2}\cdot {K}^{4} \\  & =O\cdot {K}^{4} \\  & =O\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{K}^{6}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of an Idempotent Matrix
question.worked_solution:
First, we compute ${Z}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Z}^{2} & =Z\cdot Z \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =Z\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${Z}^{2}=Z,$ so $Z$ is an idempotent matrix. 

We can use this fact to compute ${Z}^{5}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Z}^{5} & ={Z}^{2}\cdot {Z}^{2}\cdot Z \\  & =Z\cdot Z\cdot Z \\  & ={Z}^{2}\cdot Z \\  & =Z\cdot Z \\  & ={Z}^{2} \\  & =Z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Z}^{5}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Slope of the Tangent to a Parametric Curve at a Given Point
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094437/assets/9434dda63c08fc1202d16ab5410fe7061050515876ffa473d8720db39079af3e.png)

For the parametric curve 

$$
x={t}^{3}+{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{2},\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

shown above, calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=2.$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}+2t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{2t}{3{t}^{2}+2t} \\  & =\frac{2}{3t+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{2}{3(2)+2} \\  & =\frac{2}{6+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Using Standard Gaussian Elimination
question.problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned} & x+y+2z=1 \\  & 2x+3y+4z=6 \\  & 3x+3y+4z=11\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and hence solve the linear system.
question.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{aligned}].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\{\begin{aligned} & x+y+2z=1 \\  & y=4 \\  & z=-4\end{aligned}
$$

and we can apply back substitution. Substituting both $y=4$ and $z=-4$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(4)+2(-4)=1\,⟹\,x=5.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=5,y=4$, and $z=-4.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨5,4,-4⟩.$

question.knowledge_point: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Using Standard Gaussian Elimination with Row Exchanges
question.problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 5 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 & 9\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form.
question.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 5 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & -2 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & -2 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & -2 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply the $2$nd row by $-\frac{1}{3}$ and the $3$rd row by $\frac{1}{2}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & -2 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{7}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{7}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Solving a 2x2 System of Equations Using an Inverse Matrix
question.problem:
Which of the following represents the solution to the system of linear equations given below?

$$
\{\begin{aligned}8y=6 \\ -5x+6y=7\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
This system can be written as

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the solution, we need to calculate the inverse of the coefficient matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}].$
This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{6\cdot 0-(-5)\cdot 8}[\begin{aligned}6 & -8 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{40}[\begin{aligned}6 & -8 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can now represent the solution to this system, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{40}[\begin{aligned}6 & -8 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Solving a 2x2 System of Equations Using an Inverse Matrix With Reorganization
question.problem:
Which of the following represents the solution to the system of linear equations given below?

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2y=x+3 \\ 7-y=-x\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we reorganize the equations so that they are in the right order, to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-x+2y=3 \\ x-y=-7.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can represent this system of equations in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the solution, we need to calculate the inverse of the coefficient matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{(-1)\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the solution to this system as:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Expected Value of a Constant
question.worked_solution:
For any constant $a,$ we have

$$
\text{E}[a]=a.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\text{E}[{c}^{2}]={c}^{2}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Expected Value of a Scaled Random Variable
question.worked_solution:
For any constant $a$ and any random variable $X,$ we have

$$
\text{E}[aX]=a\text{E}[X].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[3X] & =3\text{E}[X] \\  & =3(-\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
